marrow__ANAT_CH23_Q001.takeaway: Central diabetes insipidus from posterior pituitary dysfunction points to diencephalon, which derives from prosencephalon.
marrow__ANAT_CH23_Q001.displayText: The scenario of polyuria and polydipsia with absence of the posterior pituitary bright spot is suggestive of central diabetes insipidus. It involves the diencephalon, which is derived from the prosencephalon. The diencephalon forms the thalamus, epithalamus, subthalamus and hypothalamus. The source MRI identifies the posterior pituitary bright spot and distinguishes the anterior and posterior pituitary.

rationales.a: Metencephalon forms pons and cerebellum, not the diencephalic structures implicated by posterior pituitary failure.
rationales.b: Myelencephalon forms the medulla; it does not give rise to diencephalon.
rationales.c: Telencephalon forms the cerebral hemispheres, while the thalamus and hypothalamus develop from diencephalon.

marrow__ANAT_CH23_Q002.takeaway: The medial thalamic surface forms the lateral wall of the third ventricle; the thalamus borders the internal capsule laterally.
marrow__ANAT_CH23_Q002.displayText: The medial surface of the thalamus forms the lateral wall, not the inferior boundary, of the third ventricle. The source gives thalamic relations: anteriorly, interventricular foramen; superiorly, stratum zonale with body of fornix and ventricle above; posteriorly, pulvinar overhanging the superior colliculus; inferiorly, the plane connecting hypothalamic sulci; medially, lateral wall of third ventricle; laterally, posterior limb of internal capsule.
emphasis: lateral wall, not the inferior boundary

rationales.a: The anterior thalamic pole does form the posterior boundary of the interventricular foramen.
rationales.b: The pulvinar overhangs the superior colliculus, a true posterior relation.
rationales.d: Posterior limb of internal capsule lies lateral to thalamus, also a true relation; option C wrongly calls the medial surface an inferior boundary.

marrow__ANAT_CH23_Q003.takeaway: The internal medullary lamina is a Y-shaped white matter sheet dividing thalamus into anterior, medial, and lateral groups.
marrow__ANAT_CH23_Q003.displayText: The marked structure X is the thalamus. The internal medullary lamina is a Y-shaped sheet of white matter dividing the thalamus into three parts: anterior, medial and lateral nuclear groups. The external medullary lamina is a sheet of white matter on the lateral surface of the thalamus and separates it from the reticular nucleus. Intralaminar nuclei lie within the internal medullary lamina, while midline nuclei lie close to the lateral walls of the third ventricle.
emphasis: dividing the thalamus into three parts

rationales.a: The external medullary lamina is white matter, not grey matter, on the lateral thalamic surface.
rationales.b: Intralaminar nuclei lie within the internal medullary lamina, not outside it.
rationales.d: The Y-shaped internal lamina creates three groups, not two.

marrow__ANAT_CH23_Q004.takeaway: The anteroventral, rather than anteromedial, nucleus is the largest anterior thalamic subdivision.
marrow__ANAT_CH23_Q004.displayText: The largest subdivision of the anterior thalamic nuclei is the anteroventral nucleus, not the anteromedial nucleus. The anterior thalamic nuclei have anteroventral, anteromedial and anterodorsal subdivisions. Major input comes through the mammillothalamic tract from mammillary nuclei of the hypothalamus. Major cortical output is to anterior limbic area, cingulate and parahippocampal gyrus. Functions include regulation of alertness and attention and acquisition of memory.

rationales.b: Mammillothalamic fibers from mammillary nuclei are a major input to anterior thalamic nuclei.
rationales.c: Anterior thalamic lesions can impair memory and cause amnesia.
rationales.d: The source includes alertness and attention regulation among anterior nuclear functions; only option A misidentifies the largest subdivision.

marrow__ANAT_CH23_Q005.takeaway: The dorsomedial thalamic nucleus connects hypothalamus with prefrontal cortex and integrates emotional context.
marrow__ANAT_CH23_Q005.displayText: The medial nucleus of the thalamus predominantly receives input from the hypothalamus and sends output to the prefrontal cortex. The medial thalamic group includes the large dorsomedial nucleus and smaller nuclei. The dorsomedial nucleus is connected internally to other thalamic nuclei and externally has major connections with prefrontal cortex and hypothalamus. Its functions include integration of somatic, visceral and olfactory sensory information and relation of this information to emotional feelings and subjective states.
emphasis: somatic, visceral and olfactory sensory information

rationales.a: Mammillary bodies and cingulate gyrus are associated with anterior limbic circuitry, not the predominant medial nucleus input-output pair asked here.
rationales.c: Substantia nigra and motor cortex describe basal ganglia motor connections, not dorsomedial thalamic connectivity.
rationales.d: Cerebellum and motor cortex are not the predominant connections of medial thalamic nuclei.

marrow__ANAT_CH23_Q006.takeaway: The lateral nuclear group is the largest thalamic division and contains dorsal and ventral nuclei.
marrow__ANAT_CH23_Q006.displayText: The largest division of the thalamus is the lateral thalamic nuclei. The lateral thalamic nuclei are further divided into dorsal and ventral nuclei.

rationales.a: Anterior nuclei are a smaller thalamic division than the extensive lateral nuclear group.
rationales.c: Medial nuclei are a distinct smaller division, not the largest group.
rationales.d: Intralaminar nuclei are embedded in the internal lamina and are not the largest thalamic division.

marrow__ANAT_CH23_Q007.takeaway: Trigeminothalamic sensory input from the face reaches the ventral posteromedial nucleus.
marrow__ANAT_CH23_Q007.displayText: The ventral posteromedial nucleus receives inputs from the trigeminothalamic pathway.

rationales.a: Ventral anterior nucleus is related to basal ganglia motor circuits, not medial lemniscal input.
rationales.b: Ventral lateral nucleus receives major cerebellar and pallidal motor input, not spinothalamic input.
rationales.c: Ventral posterolateral nucleus relays body somatic sensation; gustatory input is associated with VPM.

marrow__ANAT_CH23_Q008.takeaway: Medial geniculate auditory input comes from both ears but is stronger from the contralateral ear.
marrow__ANAT_CH23_Q008.displayText: The medial geniculate body receives auditory input from both ears, but predominantly from the contralateral ear; therefore the statement saying predominantly ipsilateral input is incorrect.

rationales.a: Intralaminar nuclei influence levels of consciousness, a correct statement.
rationales.b: This is the correct auditory laterality relation: medial geniculate receives bilateral input, predominantly contralateral.
rationales.c: Lateral geniculate relays the contralateral visual field, so this is correct; D reverses the predominant auditory side.

marrow__ANAT_CH23_Q009.takeaway: The thalamic reticular nucleus projects mainly to other thalamic nuclei rather than neocortex.
marrow__ANAT_CH23_Q009.displayText: The marked structure is the thalamus. The reticular nucleus of the thalamus does not project to the neocortex; its output is mainly to other thalamic nuclei. The source states that the other thalamic nuclei listed send output to the neocortex.
emphasis: does not project to the neocortex

rationales.a: Intralaminar nuclei do project to neocortex and participate in arousal, unlike reticular nucleus.
rationales.b: Pulvinar nuclei project to association cortex; they are not the exception.
rationales.d: Midline nuclei have cortical projections; reticular nuclei instead chiefly influence other thalamic nuclei.

marrow__ANAT_CH23_Q010.takeaway: Supraoptic nucleus vasopressin synthesis supports water conservation; lesion can produce central diabetes insipidus.
marrow__ANAT_CH23_Q010.displayText: Lesion of the supraoptic nucleus of the hypothalamus inhibits synthesis of vasopressin and can cause diabetes insipidus. The hypothalamus is part of the diencephalon below the thalamus. The source notes that anteriorly the preoptic area is included, posteriorly it merges with midbrain tegmentum, and laterally it is bounded by the internal capsule.

rationales.a: Preoptic nuclei have reproductive and thermoregulatory functions and are not the principal vasopressin source associated here.
rationales.c: Suprachiasmatic nucleus is the circadian pacemaker; damage does not produce this classic vasopressin-deficiency pattern.
rationales.d: Paraventricular nucleus also synthesizes vasopressin, but the source specifically identifies supraoptic nucleus for this question.

marrow__ANAT_CH23_Q011.takeaway: Tuber cinereum is hypothalamic, while habenular nuclei, stria medullaris, posterior commissure, and pineal gland are epithalamic.
marrow__ANAT_CH23_Q011.displayText: Tuber cinereum is not part of the epithalamus; it is part of the hypothalamus. The epithalamus consists of anterior and posterior paraventricular nuclei, medial and lateral habenular nuclei, stria medullaris thalami, posterior commissure and pineal gland.

rationales.c: Stria medullaris thalami belongs to the epithalamic complex.
rationales.d: Posterior commissure is also included in the epithalamus; tuber cinereum belongs to hypothalamus.

marrow__ANAT_CH23_Q012.takeaway: Thalamic pain syndrome follows thalamic infarction and may cause contralateral sensory loss followed by severe burning pain.
marrow__ANAT_CH23_Q012.displayText: The clinical stem of hemisensory loss with severe excruciating/burning pain is suggestive of thalamic pain syndrome (Dejerine-Roussy syndrome). The thalamus, marked B, is most likely involved. Occlusion of thalamic and thalamogeniculate branches can produce contralateral hemisensory loss that may progress to severe burning pain during recovery from thalamic infarction. The source identifies the other marks as A: caudate nucleus; C: substantia nigra; D: pons.

rationales.a: A identifies caudate nucleus, not the marked thalamus.
rationales.c: C identifies substantia nigra in midbrain, not the sensory relay lesion.
rationales.d: D identifies pons, whereas the described contralateral hemisensory loss and burning pain localize to thalamic infarction.
